patient.name: Abdi Warsame
patient.setting: Respiratory assessment unit, Royal London Hospital
patient.complaint: Six weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss, with streaks of blood in his sputum
background: Shares a two-bedroom flat in Tower Hamlets with four men
Younger brother Hamza, 14, visits most weekends
No previous illness; never had an HIV test

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with chronic cough over 3 weeks, night sweats, weight loss and haemoptysis in someone from an endemic area or on immunosuppression (anti-TNF, HIV), or an extrapulmonary form: Pott's spine, ileocaecal mass, TB meningitis, miliary TB.

points: **Cough for 6 weeks**; now streaks of blood.
Drenching **night sweats**; trousers loose, **8 kg lost**.
Tired all the time; missing shifts as a delivery driver.

visual.title: Cough duration
visual.label: Abdi 6 weeks
visual.caption: A cough beyond 3 weeks with systemic symptoms is TB until proven otherwise.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Chronic cough, haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss in a young man from an **endemic area**: pulmonary TB.

steps.lead: Abdi's illness is **Mycobacterium tuberculosis**: a granulomatous infection that is usually in the lungs but can reach almost any organ.
Abdi has two risk factors: **residence in an endemic area** and close, crowded living. His **HIV** status is unknown and must be checked.

points: Rubbery nodes in the right side of his neck.
Spine non-tender; abdomen soft, no mass.

steps.lead: Abdi has the full pulmonary picture: **cough over 3 weeks**, mild haemoptysis, fever, sweats, weight loss, cachexia, crackles and lymphadenopathy.
Abdi's spine and abdomen were examined because TB also causes **Pott's disease**, an **ileocaecal mass**, lymph node, CNS and skin disease (**lupus vulgaris**).
Untreated, Abdi risks **cavitation**, **miliary TB**, **TB meningitis** and death; his brother and flatmates are at risk too.

steps.text: A normal temperature does not exclude TB: the fever is often low-grade and evening. The **duration** (over 3 weeks) and **night sweats** carry the stem.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?' (three sputum samples for AFB smear and culture; culture is gold standard), CXR findings (upper zone, cavitation), IGRA versus Mantoux for latent TB, and the HIV test.

visual.title: Abdi's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Patchy right upper zone opacification with a cavity: classic post-primary TB.

steps.lead: Abdi's CXR shows the **upper zone** cavitating change. He can cough up sputum, so no **bronchoalveolar lavage** is needed; respiratory **PCR** speeds things up.

steps.q: Which test is the gold standard for confirming active TB?
steps.r: **Culture** is the most sensitive and identifies drug sensitivities, but takes weeks. IGRA and Mantoux only show exposure.

steps.lead: Abdi gives **three early-morning sputum samples** for AFB smear and culture. Auramine staining gives the fastest smear result.

steps.title: Abdi's sputum (48 hours)
steps.text: Smear-positive means he is **infectious**. Culture will confirm and give full sensitivities.
A positive AFB smear is **not specific**: all mycobacteria are acid-fast. PCR or culture confirms it is M. tuberculosis.

steps.title: Abdi's baseline bloods
steps.text: New HIV: this changes when antiretrovirals start.

steps.lead: Every patient tested for TB gets an **HIV test**: Abdi's is positive. Baseline U&Es, LFTs, FBC and **vision** are checked before RIPE.
His flatmates and brother Hamza are screened for **latent TB**: the UK prefers **IGRA**, especially after BCG; Mantoux is positive at **5 mm or more**.

visual.title: Flatmate's Mantoux induration
visual.label: Yusuf 11 mm
visual.caption: Measure the induration (the hard lump), not the redness, at 48 to 72 hours.

steps.title: Mantoux vs IGRA
head: Mantoux (TST)
IGRA
rows: Blood test: T cells release interferon-gamma to TB antigens
Neither test separates latent from active TB

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (RIPE for 2 months, then RI for 4 months), side-effect questions (orange urine, neuropathy, vision, gout), latent TB regimens, ART timing in HIV, and BCG for contacts.

points: Abdi is moved to a **negative-pressure side room**.
Staff wear FFP3 masks until he is smear-negative.
Public health is notified the same day.

steps.lead: Abdi is notified on suspicion and starts **RIPE** for 2 months, then **rifampicin and isoniazid** for 4 more: 6 months in total, with **pyridoxine**.

steps.title: Abdi's 6-month regimen
nodes: Month 6: complete if fully sensitive, no CNS disease
steps.caption: CNS TB needs longer treatment and steroids; drug-resistant TB needs specialist regimens.

steps.q: Why does Abdi also take pyridoxine?

steps.lead: Abdi is warned what to look for: jaundice (rifampicin, pyrazinamide), tingling feet (isoniazid), blurred or colour vision change (**ethambutol**), joint pain (pyrazinamide).

steps.title: RIPE side effects
head: Drug
Classic side effect
Exam clue
rows: 'Orange urine' is expected; also an enzyme inducer

steps.q: Week 2: Abdi's urine is orange. What is the best response?
steps.r: Orange-red urine and tears are a harmless, expected rifampicin effect. Soft contact lenses can stain.

steps.lead: Abdi's antiretrovirals are started about **4 weeks** after his TB drugs to reduce the risk of **IRIS**.

visual.title: Abdi's weight on treatment
visual.caption: Weight gain and loss of night sweats are the simplest signs that treatment is working.

steps.lead: Yusuf (Mantoux 11 mm, CXR clear, no symptoms) has **latent TB**: 3 months isoniazid plus rifampicin with pyridoxine. He can keep working.
Hamza, 14, is unvaccinated and Mantoux-negative: he is offered **BCG**. Abdi himself, HIV-positive, must not have this **live vaccine**.
Abdi's care follows **NICE NG33** and UKHSA notification guidance: notify, RIPE for 6 months, screen contacts.

steps.text: **Rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer**: it reduces the pill, warfarin and many antiretrovirals. That is when **rifabutin** is substituted.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: mechanism of each RIPE drug, why TB favours the upper lobes, why it reactivates with immunosuppression (HIV, anti-TNF), and how miliary TB spreads.

steps.lead: Abdi's bacilli are **acid-fast**, slow-growing and live inside macrophages. The **Th1** response walls them off in **granulomas**.

steps.title: From inhalation to cavity
nodes: Th1 cells release IFN-gamma; macrophages activate
Necrosis erodes into a bronchus: cavity, infectious sputum
steps.caption: This is why granulomas on biopsy and a cavity on CXR both point to TB.

steps.lead: Abdi's cavity is in the **upper lobe**: caseating granulomas break down there because **higher oxygen tension** suits this aerobic organism.

steps.q: Why does TB favour the upper lobes?
steps.r: M. tuberculosis is **aerobic**; the apices are best ventilated relative to perfusion, so oxygen tension is highest.

steps.lead: Abdi may have caught TB in Somalia years ago; his new **HIV** weakened cell-mediated immunity, letting latent TB **reactivate**.
With a CD4 of 180, Abdi is at risk of **miliary TB**: bloodstream spread seeding millet-seed granulomas, plus extrapulmonary spread to bone, nodes and meninges.
Each RIPE drug hits a different target, so together they kill bacilli and prevent **resistance** emerging.

steps.title: How the RIPE drugs work
head: Drug
Mechanism
rows: Active in the **acidic** environment inside macrophages

steps.text: Anti-TNF drugs such as **infliximab** break granulomas down: screen for latent TB (IGRA) before starting them.

mcq.r: TB is a granulomatous infection with **M. tuberculosis**.

mcq.q: Which drug class notably increases TB risk?
mcq.r: TNF holds granulomas together; anti-TNF drugs let latent TB reactivate.
Skeletal TB of the spine is **Pott's disease**.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard test for active TB?
mcq.r: Culture is most sensitive but slow.

mcq.q: Which test is preferred for latent TB in a BCG-vaccinated person?
mcq.r: BCG gives false-positive Mantoux results; IGRA is not affected.

mcq.q: Where is the classic CXR change in pulmonary TB?
mcq.r: Patchy or fibronodular **upper zone** opacification with cavitation.

mcq.q: What is the standard regimen for active non-CNS TB?
Which TB drug causes red-green colour blindness?
mcq.r: Ethambutol causes **optic neuropathy**; check vision before starting.

mcq.q: When should antiretrovirals start in HIV with newly treated TB?

mcq.r: Mycolic acid is the waxy cell wall layer.

Latent TB: asymptomatic, non-infectious, positive screening test, no active disease

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem hides the risk factor in the social history or drug list.

points.why: Test every TB patient for HIV.

points.p: Travel to or residence in an endemic area

points.why: Also prison, drug and alcohol use.

prompts.q: How does pulmonary TB present, and what do you find on examination?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: duration over 3 weeks is the key number.

points.why: The threshold that should trigger TB testing.

prompts.q: Name the extrapulmonary forms of TB and their clues.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: TB is the great mimic outside the lung.

points.p: GI TB: abdominal pain, ileocaecal mass

prompts.q: What are the complications of TB?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: subacute meningitis in a contact from a high-prevalence country is TB until proven otherwise.

points.p: TB meningitis: subacute fever, headache, confusion
points.why: CSF: lymphocytes, high protein, very low glucose.
Treatment is highly effective if completed.

prompts.q: How do you confirm active pulmonary TB, and what does the CXR show?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three samples, smear and culture; culture is gold standard.

points.why: BAL or gastric aspirate (children) if no sputum.

points.p: Mycobacterial culture: gold standard, most sensitive, slow
CXR: upper zone patchy/fibronodular opacity, cavitation

prompts.q: What else must every TB patient have before treatment?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: HIV test and baseline vision.

points.why: Changes ART timing and drug choice.
Three of the four drugs are hepatotoxic risks.

prompts.q: How is latent TB tested for, and which test is preferred?

points.why: Measure the induration, not the redness.

prompts.q: What is the treatment for active TB, and what do you add?

points.p: RIPE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the symptom in the stem to the drug.

points.p: Rifampicin: hepatotoxicity, orange-red urine and tears

prompts.q: How do you treat latent TB, HIV co-infection and protect contacts?

points.p: Latent: 3 months isoniazid + rifampicin, or 6 months isoniazid
Latent TB is not infectious: no work restriction
HIV: delay ART about 4 weeks to reduce IRIS
BCG for Mantoux-negative unvaccinated contacts under 35
BCG is live: not in immunosuppression

prompts.q: Why does TB form granulomas, cavitate in the upper lobes and reactivate, and how do the drugs work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: Th1, oxygen, immunity, cell wall.

points.p: Upper lobes: higher oxygen tension for an aerobic organism

points.why: Latent bacilli lie dormant in granulomas.

points.p: Isoniazid: mycolic acid; rifampicin: RNA polymerase

glossary.TB: Tuberculosis: infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, usually of the lungs.
glossary.Mycobacterium tuberculosis: Slow-growing, aerobic, acid-fast bacillus that causes tuberculosis.
glossary.latent TB: Contained TB infection: positive screening test, no symptoms, not infectious.
glossary.granuloma: A cluster of activated macrophages and lymphocytes that walls off an organism.
glossary.caseating necrosis: Cheese-like dead tissue at the centre of a TB granuloma.
glossary.cavitation: Formation of an air-filled hole in the lung where necrotic tissue has drained away.
glossary.miliary TB: Bloodstream spread of TB seeding many tiny millet-seed granulomas through the organs.
glossary.Pott's disease: Tuberculosis of the spine, causing back pain and vertebral collapse.
glossary.lupus vulgaris: The commonest form of skin TB: papules enlarging into scaly red plaques.
glossary.ileocaecal: Where the end of the small bowel joins the caecum; the usual site of GI TB.
glossary.cachexia: Severe wasting of muscle and fat from chronic illness.
glossary.AFB: Acid-fast bacilli: bacteria that keep a stain after acid washing, such as mycobacteria.
glossary.acid-fast: Retains stain after acid washing because of a waxy mycolic acid cell wall.
glossary.Ziehl-Neelsen: A stain that shows acid-fast bacilli as red rods on a blue background.
glossary.auramine: A fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli; the fastest smear method.
glossary.bronchoalveolar lavage: Washing a lung segment with saline at bronchoscopy to collect a sample.
glossary.BAL: Bronchoalveolar lavage: a lung washing sample taken at bronchoscopy.
glossary.gastric aspirate: Stomach fluid aspirated in the morning to find swallowed TB bacilli, used in young children.
glossary.Mantoux: Tuberculin skin test; the induration is read at 48 to 72 hours, 5 mm or more is positive.
glossary.induration: The firm, raised area of skin measured in a Mantoux test; redness is ignored.
glossary.IGRA: Interferon-gamma release assay: a blood test for TB exposure, not affected by BCG.
glossary.BCG: Bacillus Calmette-Guérin: a live attenuated TB vaccine.
glossary.RIPE: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol: the first-line TB regimen.
glossary.rifampicin: TB drug that inhibits RNA polymerase; turns urine orange and induces liver enzymes.
glossary.isoniazid: TB drug that blocks mycolic acid synthesis; causes peripheral neuropathy.
glossary.pyrazinamide: TB drug active in acidic macrophages; causes hepatitis and gout.
glossary.ethambutol: TB drug that blocks arabinogalactan synthesis; causes optic neuropathy.
glossary.rifabutin: A rifamycin with fewer drug interactions, used in place of rifampicin.
glossary.pyridoxine: Vitamin B6, given with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
glossary.peripheral neuropathy: Nerve damage causing tingling, numbness or burning in the hands and feet.
glossary.optic neuropathy: Damage to the optic nerve causing blurred vision or loss of colour vision.
glossary.hyperuricaemia: High blood uric acid, which can cause gout.
glossary.enzyme inducer: A drug that speeds up liver metabolism of other drugs, lowering their levels.
glossary.IRIS: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome: inflammatory flare when immunity recovers on ART.
glossary.ART: Antiretroviral therapy: the drug combination used to treat HIV.
glossary.CD4 count: Number of CD4 helper T cells; a low count shows HIV-related immunosuppression.
glossary.infliximab: An anti-TNF antibody for Crohn's and arthritis that can reactivate latent TB.
glossary.anti-TNF: Drugs blocking tumour necrosis factor; TNF is needed to keep granulomas intact.
glossary.Th1: T helper 1 cells, which activate macrophages with interferon-gamma to control TB.
glossary.mycolic acid: Waxy fatty acid in the mycobacterial cell wall, target of isoniazid.
glossary.arabinogalactan: A cell wall polysaccharide in mycobacteria, target of ethambutol.
glossary.negative-pressure room: An isolation room whose air flows inwards, stopping airborne spread.
glossary.FFP3: A high-filtration respirator mask worn by staff caring for infectious TB.
glossary.smear-positive: Acid-fast bacilli seen on sputum microscopy; the patient is highly infectious.

technique.stem: A 41 year old man who moved from Pakistan 5 years ago has a 3 month history of right-sided abdominal pain, fever, night sweats and weight loss. His brother is being treated for tuberculosis. There is a tender mass in the right iliac fossa. Chest X-ray shows fibronodular shadowing at the right apex.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question with an abdominal mass and systemic symptoms.

clues: His brother is being treated for tuberculosis
mass in the right iliac fossa
fibronodular shadowing at the right apex
steps.x: Endemic country, TB contact, B symptoms, **ileocaecal mass**, apical shadowing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: GI (ileocaecal) TB.

elim: Follows days of appendicitis, not 3 months of sweats and weight loss.
Possible at older ages, but sweats, a TB contact and apical shadowing point to TB.
Can give an RIF mass, but does not explain the TB contact and apical shadowing.
Causes B symptoms, but the TB contact and apical CXR change fit TB better.

steps.x: **D. Ileocaecal TB.** Rule: RIF mass + TB risk + apical CXR change = GI TB.

technique.stem: A 36 year old woman from Nepal has a 5 week history of productive cough, evening fevers and weight loss. Chest X-ray shows left upper zone opacification with a cavity. Her first sputum sample shows acid-fast bacilli on auramine staining.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: 'Confirm the diagnosis' means the gold standard.

clues: left upper zone opacification with a cavity
steps.x: Smear-positive, but AFB is not specific to M. tuberculosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mycobacterial culture: gold standard, most sensitive, gives sensitivities.

elim: Shows the extent of disease but cannot identify the organism.
Shows exposure; cannot distinguish latent from active TB.
Shows exposure only, and is affected by BCG.
Smear is not specific: all mycobacteria are acid-fast.

steps.x: **D. Culture.** Rule: smear suggests, culture confirms.

technique.stem: A 27 year old man has smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis that is fully sensitive on PCR. He has no neurological symptoms. His HIV test is negative and his LFTs and visual acuity are normal. He is about to start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate additional medication?

steps.x: An 'additional medication' question alongside RIPE.
Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy; it is prevented routinely.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6).

elim: Not needed with RIPE.
Steroids are added for TB meningitis or pericarditis, not uncomplicated pulmonary TB.
A substitute for rifampicin when interactions matter, not an addition.
Not part of standard TB treatment.

steps.x: **C. Pyridoxine.** Rule: isoniazid always comes with B6.

technique.stem: A 50 year old man with pulmonary tuberculosis asks why his chest X-ray shows a cavity at the top of his right lung rather than at the base. He has never smoked and has no other lung disease.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the upper lobe location?
o: Greater blood flow at the apices
Higher oxygen tension favours the aerobic organism
Lower oxygen tension favours the organism
More lymphatic tissue at the apices

steps.x: A mechanism question about location.

clues: cavity at the top of his right lung
steps.x: Apex has a high V/Q ratio, so the highest alveolar oxygen tension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Higher oxygen tension favours the aerobic M. tuberculosis.

elim: Aspiration hits the lower lobes and posterior segments.
Perfusion is actually lower at the apices.
The reverse: M. tuberculosis is aerobic.
Not the reason; oxygen tension is.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: TB is aerobic, so it lives at the apex.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man who is homeless has a 2 month history of cough, sweats at night and weight loss. He has coughed up streaks of blood. There are crackles at the left apex. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Left upper zone opacification with cavitation.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Homelessness, a chronic cough with haemoptysis, night sweats and weight loss, and an upper zone cavity are pulmonary TB. Lung abscess and aspiration are acute and usually lower zone.

steps.x: Diagnosis with a chest X-ray.

clues: sweats at night and weight loss
steps.x: Homelessness, chronic course, B symptoms, haemoptysis, apical crackles, apical cavity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pulmonary TB.

elim: Acute, lower lobe, with a risk such as reduced consciousness.
Years of daily copious sputum, not 2 months of sweats and weight loss.
Swinging fever and foul sputum, usually after aspiration.
Bilateral hilar nodes, not an apical cavity.

steps.x: **D. Pulmonary TB.** Chronic cough + B symptoms + upper zone cavity.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman with Crohn's disease started infliximab 4 months ago. She now has 5 weeks of cough, fevers and 5 kg weight loss. She did not have latent TB screening before starting. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows right upper zone patchy opacification.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab allow latent TB to reactivate; a subacute cough, fever, weight loss and upper zone change fit TB. Pneumocystis is bilateral and perihilar.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a patient on immunosuppression.

clues: 5 weeks of cough, fevers and 5 kg weight loss
did not have latent TB screening
steps.x: Anti-TNF without screening; subacute cough, fever, weight loss; upper zone change.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Reactivation of latent TB due to infliximab.

elim: Would cause bowel symptoms, not cough and upper zone shadowing.
Diffuse changes without a classic upper zone TB pattern and weight loss.
Dry cough, desaturation on exertion, bilateral perihilar change.
Acute over days, lobar, not 5 weeks with weight loss.

steps.x: **D. TB reactivation.** Rule: anti-TNF + chronic cough = TB; screen with IGRA first.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man from Bangladesh has a 4 month history of worsening mid-back pain, night sweats and weight loss. There is a tender angular deformity of the lower thoracic spine. Leg power is normal. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Spine X-ray shows destruction of two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Two adjacent vertebrae with disc destruction, a gibbus deformity and night sweats in someone from an endemic area is spinal TB (Pott's disease). Metastases usually spare the disc.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a spinal lesion with systemic symptoms.

clues: two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them
steps.x: Endemic country, B symptoms, gibbus, two vertebrae plus the disc between.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Spinal TB (Pott's disease).

elim: Young man with inflammatory low back stiffness, not vertebral destruction and sweats.
Usually spares the disc and needs a primary cancer.
Older patients, lytic lesions with anaemia and renal impairment.
Low-trauma fracture in older patients, without sweats or disc loss.

steps.x: **E. Pott's disease.** Infection crosses the disc; tumour spares it.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman who arrived from Ethiopia a year ago has a 3 week history of headache, fever and increasing confusion. She is drowsy, with neck stiffness and a left sixth nerve palsy. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Lumbar puncture results are shown.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A subacute meningitis with cranial nerve palsy and lymphocytic CSF, very high protein and very low glucose in someone from a high-prevalence country is TB meningitis.

steps.x: Diagnosis using CSF results.
**Subacute**, endemic country, cranial nerve palsy, lymphocytes, high protein, very low glucose.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: TB meningitis.

elim: Acute over hours, with neutrophils in the CSF.
Possible in advanced HIV, but no HIV is mentioned; India ink would be positive.
Acute, temporal lobe features, CSF glucose normal.
Normal CSF glucose and a milder illness.

steps.x: **D. TB meningitis.** Subacute + lymphocytic CSF + very low glucose.

practice.stem: A 29 year old man with untreated HIV (CD4 count 60 cells/µL) has 3 weeks of fever, breathlessness and weight loss. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows numerous 1 to 2 mm nodules evenly scattered through both lungs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Innumerable uniform 1 to 2 mm nodules in a profoundly immunosuppressed patient are miliary TB, from haematogenous spread. Pneumocystis gives perihilar ground-glass change.

steps.x: Diagnosis with a described CXR in immunosuppression.

clues: numerous 1 to 2 mm nodules evenly scattered through both lungs
steps.x: Profound immunosuppression and **millet-seed** nodules = haematogenous spread.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Miliary TB.

elim: Nodular and peribronchial, often with skin lesions, not uniform millet seeds.
Bilateral perihilar ground-glass change, not tiny discrete nodules.
Bilateral hilar nodes; not a febrile illness in advanced HIV.
Lobar consolidation, acute onset.

steps.x: **B. Miliary TB.** Tiny uniform nodules everywhere = bloodstream spread.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man started treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis 6 weeks ago. He now finds his vision blurred and cannot tell red from green on his football team's kit. His pupils react normally. His BP is 130/82 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm.
practice.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Ethambutol causes toxic optic neuropathy, with blurred vision and red-green colour blindness; stop it and refer urgently. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy.

steps.x: A 'most likely cause' question about a drug side effect.
Red-green colour vision loss = optic neuropathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ethambutol.

elim: Mainly peripheral neuropathy.
Hepatotoxicity, gout and arthralgia.
Given to prevent neuropathy; it does not cause visual loss.
Hepatotoxicity and orange secretions, not colour blindness.

steps.x: **A. Ethambutol.** Rule: ethambutol = eyes; check vision at baseline.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman from the Philippines has a 6 week history of productive cough, evening fevers and weight loss. Her chest X-ray shows right upper zone opacification with cavitation. She is producing sputum.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Three sputum samples for AFB smear and culture
practice.e: Three early-morning sputum samples for AFB smear and culture confirm active TB; bronchoalveolar lavage is used only if no sputum. IGRA and Mantoux cannot diagnose active disease.

steps.x: Confirming active TB in a patient who can produce sputum.

clues: right upper zone opacification with cavitation
steps.x: Producing sputum, so the least invasive confirmatory test.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Three (early-morning) sputum samples for AFB smear and mycobacterial culture.

elim: Only if she cannot produce sputum.
Shows extent, not the organism.
Shows exposure; cannot distinguish latent from active TB.
Shows exposure only.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: active TB is confirmed by sputum, not IGRA or Mantoux.

practice.stem: A 26 year old nurse had the BCG vaccine as a child. A patient she cared for 3 weeks ago has smear-positive pulmonary TB. She is well with no cough, fever or weight loss.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to screen her for latent TB?
practice.e: IGRA is preferred in the UK for latent TB, particularly after BCG, which makes the Mantoux test less reliable. Sputum tests look for active disease.

steps.x: A latent TB screening question.

clues: had the BCG vaccine as a child
She is well with no cough
steps.x: Asymptomatic, BCG-vaccinated contact.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IGRA, preferred in the UK, especially after BCG.

elim: Done if screening is positive, to exclude active disease; it does not detect latent TB.
Less reliable after BCG, which causes false positives.
She has no symptoms and no sputum; this tests active disease.
Tests active disease, not latent infection.

steps.x: **B. IGRA.** Rule: BCG ruins the Mantoux; use IGRA.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man has smear-positive, fully sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis without neurological involvement. His HIV test is negative. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 122/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Baseline LFTs and vision are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: RIPE for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months
practice.e: Active non-CNS TB is treated with RIPE for 2 months then rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months. Isoniazid alone or 3 months of RI are latent TB regimens.

steps.x: Initial management of active pulmonary TB.
Active, non-CNS, sensitive TB.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: RIPE 2 months then RI 4 months: 6 months total, with pyridoxine.

elim: A latent TB regimen, not active disease.
A latent TB regimen.
Too short: the continuation phase is essential.
12 months is for CNS TB, and then only 2 months of all four drugs.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: 2 + 4 = 6 months for non-CNS TB.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and, at the same time, HIV with a CD4 count of 210 cells/µL. She has started rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol today. She asks when she can begin HIV treatment.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate timing for antiretroviral therapy?
o: About 4 weeks after starting TB treatment
After completing 6 months of TB treatment
Only if the CD4 count falls below 50
Today, at the same time as TB treatment
practice.e: ART is delayed about 4 weeks after starting TB treatment to reduce immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. It should not wait for the end of TB treatment.

started rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol today

TB treatment should not be delayed.

steps.x: **A. About 4 weeks.** Rule: TB drugs first, ART later, to avoid IRIS.

practice.stem: A 28 year old flatmate of a man with smear-positive pulmonary TB has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. He has no symptoms and his chest X-ray is normal. His HIV test is negative and he takes no regular medication. He works in a bank.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Exclude him from work until treated
practice.e: Latent TB is treated with 3 months of isoniazid and rifampicin (with pyridoxine), or 6 months of isoniazid if rifamycins are contraindicated. It is not infectious, so he keeps working.

steps.x: Latent TB; no reason to avoid rifamycins.

steps.x: 3 months of isoniazid plus rifampicin, with pyridoxine.

Latent TB in a young contact should be treated.

steps.x: **C. 3 months isoniazid + rifampicin.** Isoniazid alone for 6 months if rifamycins cannot be used.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis is told that one of his drugs works by blocking synthesis of the waxy mycolic acid layer of the mycobacterial cell wall. He has developed tingling in both feet.
practice.q: Which drug works by this mechanism?
practice.e: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and causes peripheral neuropathy, prevented by pyridoxine. Ethambutol blocks arabinogalactan; rifampicin blocks RNA polymerase.
